blogs.title: The Red Path Confusion: When Contradictory Expert Testimony Destroys a Patent Verdict
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's reversal of the infringement verdict on US Patent '134, driven by Dr. Wells' contradictory testimony regarding signal mapping. With a jury relying on an expert who mapped "signals of interest" to paths that physically do not exist during sampling, this analysis explores how the Court applied the "substantial evidence" standard to fact-finding. The post highlights how expert testimony inconsistently answering "two vs. one" on cross-examination failed to meet the high bar required to sustain a finding of infringement under the Fifth Circuit's regional standard adopted by the Federal Circuit.

blogs.title: Three Signals, Four Inputs, Seven Multiplications: The Struggle to Match Patent Claims to Technical Reality
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent dispute, this post examines how the Court evaluated the accused product's multiplications against claim language. It breaks down the evidentiary gap where appellants argued Finesse surrendered claim scope by amending claims to "three" when the accused device only used "two" inputs. The article discusses the difficulty of proving complex technical functionality (seven multiplications) when expert testimony maps limited mathematical operations to broad claim counts, illustrating the perils of vague claim constructions in method-of-use patents.

blogs.title: Reversing Facts, Not Law: The Federal Circuit's High Bar for "Substantial Evidence",
blogs.description: This overview covers the legal standard used to reverse the denial of JMOL. Discussing the *Wi-LAN* precedent cited in the opinion, this post explains why factual findings requiring "more than reasonable jurors could not arrive at any contrary conclusion" are so difficult to meet for patentees. It contrasts the application of this high evidentiary threshold with claim construction, offering guidance to litigators on when to argue for judgment as a matter of law versus new trials on facts.
